[[File:David Eby - 2022 (52507022370) (cropped).png|thumb|[[David Eby]] has been premier of British Columbia since 2022.]]
The [[premier of British Columbia]] is the [[first minister]] for the [[Provinces and territories of Canada|Canadian province]] of [[British Columbia]]. The province was a British crown colony governed by the [[governors of British Columbia]]<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.britishcolumbia.com/history/ |title=History and Heritage of British Columbia |publisher=BritishColumbia.com |access-date=November 5, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081102193708/http://www.britishcolumbia.com/history/ |archive-date=November 2, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> before joining [[Canadian Confederation]] in 1871.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/confederation/023001-2185-e.html |title=British Columbia – Canadian Confederation |publisher=Library and Archives Canada |access-date=November 5, 2008 |date=August 9, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080621230955/http://www.collectionscanada.gc.ca/confederation/023001-2185-e.html |archive-date=June 21, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Since then, it has had a [[unicameral]] [[Westminster System|Westminster-style]] [[parliamentary government]], in which the premier is the leader of the party that controls the most seats in the [[Legislative Assembly of British Columbia|legislative assembly]]. The premier is British Columbia's [[head of government]], and the [[Monarchy of Canada|{{lcfirst:{{Canadian monarch, current|title=*}}}} of Canada]] is its [[head of state]] and is represented by the [[Lieutenant Governor of British Columbia|lieutenant governor of British Columbia]]. The premier picks a cabinet from the elected members to form the [[Executive Council of British Columbia]] and presides over that body.<ref name="office">{{cite web|url=http://www.gov.bc.ca/govt/lieutenant_governor_legislature.html|title=The Office of the Lieutenant Governor and the Legislature – Province of British Columbia|publisher=Province of British Columbia|access-date=November 5, 2008}}</ref>

Members are first elected to the legislature during [[List of British Columbia general elections|general elections]]. General elections must be conducted every four years from the date of the last election. An election may take place before the four-year mark if the governing party loses the confidence of the legislature by the defeat of a supply bill or the passage of a no-confidence motion, provided that there is no alternative configuration in the legislature that the lieutenant governor believes can command confidence.{{efn|''See the [[2017 British Columbia general election]] and aftermath.''}}<ref name="office" />

Before 1903, British Columbia did not use a party system; instead, premiers of British Columbia had no official party affiliation and were chosen by elected members of the legislative assembly from among themselves. Candidates ran as "Government", "Opposition", "Independent", or in formulations such as "Opposition independent", indicating their respective positions to the incumbent regime.

British Columbia has had 36 individuals serve as premier since joining Confederation, of which 14 individuals had no party affiliation, three were [[British Columbia Conservative Party|Conservatives]], eight were [[British Columbia Liberal Party|Liberals]], four were [[British Columbia Social Credit Party|Socreds]], and seven were [[British Columbia New Democratic Party|New Democrats]]. The first premier was [[John Foster McCreight]], who was inaugurated in 1871. [[Joseph Martin (Canadian politician)|Joseph Martin]] spent the shortest time in office, at 106 days. At over twenty years, [[W. A. C. Bennett]] spent the longest time in office and is the only premier to serve in more than five parliaments. The incumbent premier is [[David Eby]], who was sworn in on November 18, 2022.

|accomplishments = Introduced housing reforms permitting higher-density residential development, particularly near public transit, restricted [[short-term rental]]s, and implemented a [[home flipping]] tax. Expanded access to free prescription contraception and publicly funded [[in vitro fertilisation]]. Oversaw changes to the province's drug decriminalization pilot project, including restrictions on public drug use. Led the NDP to a narrow majority in the [[2024 British Columbia general election]]. Introduced legislation to expedite major infrastructure and renewable energy projects and measures responding to [[Tariffs in the second Trump administration|United States tariffs]].
|references      = {{efn|Eby called a [[2026 British Columbia general election|snap election]] for October 24, 2026, less than two years into his government's four-year mandate. Eby cited economic threats from the United States under President [[Donald Trump]] as justification for the early election. The election was called amid divisions within the opposition [[Conservative Party of British Columbia]], whose leader, [[Kerry-Lynne Findlay]], had resigned two days earlier.<ref>{{cite news |last=Depner |first=Wolfgang |title=B.C. Premier Eby calls early election for Oct. 24, says Trump is 'existential' threat |url=https://vancouver.citynews.ca/2026/09/22/b-c-premier-eby-to-deliver-address-amid-rumours-of-possible-election-call/ |work=The Canadian Press |date=September 22, 2026 |access-date=November 1, 2026}}</ref>}}
